title: God Has Spoken by His Son

verses.text: On many past occasions and in many different ways, God spoke to our fathers through the prophets.
But in these last days He has spoken to us by His Son, whom He appointed heir of all things, and through whom He made the universe.

The Son is the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of His nature, upholding all things by His powerful word. After He had provided purification for sins, He sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high.
So He became as far superior to the angels as the name He has inherited is excellent beyond theirs.
For to which of the angels did God ever say: "You are My Son; today I have become Your Father"? Or again: "I will be His Father, and He will be My Son"?
And again, when God brings His firstborn into the world, He says: "Let all God's angels worship Him."
Now about the angels He says: "He makes His angels winds, His servants flames of fire."
But about the Son He says: "Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever, and justice is the scepter of Your kingdom.
You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness; therefore God, Your God, has anointed You above Your companions with the oil of joy."
And: "In the beginning, O Lord, You laid the foundations of the earth, and the heavens are the work of Your hands.
They will perish, but You remain; they will all wear out like a garment.
You will roll them up like a robe; like a garment they will be changed; but You remain the same, and Your years will never end."
Yet to which of the angels did God ever say: "Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet"?
Are not the angels ministering spirits sent to serve those who will inherit salvation?

context.author: Unknown. The letter does not name its author. Paul, Barnabas, Apollos, and others have been suggested.
context.genre: A sermon in letter form, rich with Old Testament quotations
context.audience: People the writer knows well (13:7, 19, 23), probably Jewish Christians, who have suffered for their faith (10:32-34) and are tempted to drift away.
context.setting: The letter begins without a greeting. It opens like a sermon with a majestic sentence: God spoke long ago through the prophets, but now through a Son. The writer then presents a chain of Old Testament quotations to prove that the Son is far above the angels.
context.custom: Many Jews believed the law was given through angels (Acts 7:53; Galatians 3:19), so showing the Son is greater than angels was showing he is greater than the law’s mediators.
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 2 gives the first warning against drifting away and begins to show why the Son became human.
context.timelineBible: The writer quotes Psalm 2:7, 2 Samuel 7:14, Deuteronomy 32:43, Psalm 104:4, Psalm 45:6-7, Psalm 102:25-27, and Psalm 110:1. All are read as speaking of the Son.
context.sparkNotes: In the past God spoke by the prophets, but now by a Son, through whom he made the world. He is the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature, upholding the universe, and has sat down at the right hand of the Majesty. He is better than the angels, as shown by Scripture: no angel was ever told, “You are my Son.” Angels are ministering spirits.

translation.meaning: The stamp on a coin or seal. The English “character” comes from it.
Shining out from a source, as light from the sun.

overview.summary: God has spoken finally through his Son, who is the radiance of God’s glory and far greater than the angels.
overview.settingLine: Written to Jewish believers under pressure.

history.t: In Jewish tradition the law was given through angels (Acts 7:53; Galatians 3:19). So the writer first shows that the Son is above the angels, then that he is above Moses and the priests who served under the law.

The letter quotes the Old Testament in its Greek form (the Septuagint) almost every time. Some quotations, such as the one in 1:6, follow the Greek wording and not the Hebrew. This fits readers who read Greek, in a city where Jews used the Greek Bible.

customs.t: To sit at the king's right hand was to share his honor and rule (1 Kings 2:19; Psalm 110:1). Hebrews says the Son sat down there after he made purification for sins.
The Greek word charaktēr comes from the engraver's tool and the mark it leaves, as on a coin or seal. The Son is the exact representation of God's being (1:3).

archaeology.h: Angels in the Dead Sea Scrolls
archaeology.t: The Songs of the Sabbath Sacrifice, found at Qumran and copied in the 1st centuries BC and AD, describe angelic priests serving in a heavenly sanctuary. Hebrews shares the interest in angels and a heavenly sanctuary, but argues that the Son is above them all.

Hebrews usually quotes the Greek Old Testament. That text survives in great Greek Bibles of the 4th century such as Codex Vaticanus and Codex Sinaiticus and in older papyri. Codex Vaticanus is also one of the oldest copies of Hebrews itself.

overview.discussion: The writer says God has spoken most fully in a person, not a book or a vision. What changes if I think of Jesus as God’s clearest word?
overview.book: The letter to the Hebrews · 13 chapters. A polished sermon showing that Jesus fulfills and surpasses the old covenant.
overview.author: Unknown

historicalImage.caption: A page of Codex Vaticanus, a Greek Bible copied in the 4th century and kept in the Vatican Library. It shows the end of 2 Thessalonians (3:11-18) and the opening of Hebrews (1:1-2:2). In this manuscript Hebrews follows 2 Thessalonians, among the letters of Paul, although the letter itself never names its author.
